lesson.menu_title: How a Canadian Classroom Works — Rubrics and Group Work
lesson.menu_desc: Reading a marking rubric and surviving a group project -- 39 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- How a Canadian Classroom Works: Rubrics and Group Work
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Laís Paludetto Rodrigues | Lesson 6 -- How a Canadian Classroom Works

listenings.text: Right, listen carefully, because this is the part people get wrong every single year. The project is done in groups of four and it is marked in two separate ways. Half of the mark is given to the group, for the final presentation, and half is given to you individually, for your section and for how you worked in the team. That second half is decided by two things: my notes, and the peer review form that is filled in by the other three people in your group. So no, you cannot disappear for three weeks and turn up on presentation day. Drafts are collected on the fifteenth and the final version is due on the twenty-ninth. Everything is submitted through the portal, and everything is checked for plagiarism automatically.

Hey, it's Owen, from the group. So I looked at the rubric properly and we have been doing this wrong. The biggest section is not the content, it is the analysis, which is worth forty percent on its own. We have written a lot of facts and almost no argument. Also the presentation has to be twelve minutes, not twenty, and marks are taken off if you go over. I've put the slides in the shared folder. Could you take the second part, the comparison? Your section was the clearest one in the draft, honestly, and mine was described by the teacher as, and I quote, a list. Anyway, let me know if you want to swap.

extra_audio.text: The teacher hands out the rubric and explains how the project is marked. The group meets at lunch and each person is given one section. Lais writes the comparison and sends it to the shared folder. The drafts are collected on the fifteenth and comments come back a week later. On the last day the presentation is delivered and the peer review forms are filled in.

paras: This project is marked out of one hundred. Fifty marks are given to the group for the final presentation and fifty are given to each student individually. The individual half is decided by the teacher's notes and by the peer review forms, which are completed by the other members of the group.

Content and research, twenty marks. Sources are listed at the end and at least two of them are not websites. Work that is copied from another source without a reference is treated as plagiarism, and the whole assignment is checked automatically.

Analysis, forty marks. This is the largest section and it is the one that is misunderstood most often. Facts alone are not analysis. An argument is expected: what the facts mean, why they matter, and what somebody who disagreed with you would say.

Presentation and teamwork, forty marks. The talk must last twelve minutes. Marks are taken off if you go over. Drafts are collected on the fifteenth and comments are returned within a week. The final version is submitted through the portal by nine in the evening on the twenty-ninth.
reading.source: Burnaby Secondary -- Social Studies 11, term project

gist.prompt: What is this document mainly about?
choices: The subject the students have to research
Exactly how the marks are divided and what each section is worth
A list of the sources students should use

items: Half of the mark is individual.
Fifty marks are given to the group and fifty are given to each student individually.
Analysis is worth more than content and research.
Analysis, forty marks. This is the largest section.
Only the teacher decides the individual half.
The individual half is decided by the teacher's notes and by the peer review forms.
Going over twelve minutes has no consequence.
The talk must last twelve minutes. Marks are taken off if you go over.

items.situation: You do not understand how the project is marked. Ask the teacher, using the document in front of you.
tips: How is the individual half decided?
Is the analysis section worth more than the others?

items.situation: One person in your group has done nothing for two weeks. Bring it up with the group, not with the teacher, first.
tips: Can we go through who is doing what again?
The drafts are collected on Friday.
Which section would you rather take?

items.situation: You are asked to explain your section to the group in thirty seconds. Do it, in the passive where it fits.
tips: My part is based on two sources.

items.situation: You got your feedback back and you do not understand one comment. Ask about it.
tips: I'm not sure what this comment means.
Could you show me an example of what you expected?
How could I improve that part?

items.situation: You are worried that your English will cost you marks. Ask the teacher directly and calmly.
tips: Is the mark affected by grammar mistakes?
I'd rather know now than after.
What should I focus on first?

items.situation: The group wants to divide the presentation and nobody wants the introduction. Volunteer, and say why.
tips: If I go first, I'll be less nervous.
